scope: Navigation and travel, route plotting, fuel-star planning, supercruise, gravity wells, Supercruise Overcharge, orbital cruise and glide, neutron/white-dwarf supercharging, FSD injections, and long-range travel workflow used by the Mongrels Field Manual and Ask the Mongrels.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Use Fastest Routes for normal travel, Economical Routes when fuel conservation or system coverage matters, and enable jet-cone boosts only when the ship is equipped and the pilot intends to use neutron/white-dwarf supercharging.
details: Fastest Routes favors longer jumps and fewer systems; Economical Routes favors shorter, more fuel-efficient jumps.
The route plotter uses the ship's current jump capability, so cargo mass, module mass and fuel load can affect whether a leg is reachable.
Star-class filters can be used to keep routes on scoopable stars when the corresponding route-filter option is enabled.
Jet-cone routing requires a fuel scoop because the FSD is supercharged by flying through a neutron-star or white-dwarf jet cone while scooping.

keywords: o b a f g k m
entries.ruleOfThumb: The normal scoopable stellar classes are O, B, A, F, G, K and M — commonly remembered as KGBFOAM.
details: A fuel scoop works while flying close enough to a scoopable star in supercruise.
Brown dwarfs, neutron stars, white dwarfs and many other stellar types are not normal refuelling stars even though some can be used for FSD supercharging.
For long-range travel, route filtering to scoopable stars greatly reduces the chance of stranding yourself between refuelling opportunities.
Do not wait until the tank is nearly empty before checking the next scoopable stop in sparse regions.

entries.topic: Jump Range, Cargo Mass & Fuel Mass
entries.ruleOfThumb: Jump range is mass-sensitive. Cargo, fuel and fitted modules all count, so a route that works empty may fail when the ship is heavily laden.
details: Cargo mass directly reduces hyperspace range.
Fuel carried in the main tank also contributes mass; in extreme sparse-space situations, carrying less fuel can marginally increase maximum single-jump reach.
Check the ship's laden/current jump range rather than relying only on an empty-build number from a ship builder.
A route can become unavailable after loading cargo even when the destination itself did not change.

keywords: why am i slow in supercruise
entries.ruleOfThumb: If full throttle feels inexplicably slow in supercruise, look at nearby gravity wells. Stars, planets and moons limit supercruise acceleration even when the throttle is at 100%.
details: Supercruise speed is constrained by the gravity of nearby massive bodies.
Climbing away from a planet, moon or star lets the ship accelerate much more quickly.
A direct line through multiple gravity wells can be slower than a slightly wider route above or below the orbital plane.
The slowdown is not necessarily a ship fault or an FSD problem.

entries.ruleOfThumb: For a simple reliable approach, stay at full throttle until the ETA reaches about 6-7 seconds, then reduce to roughly 75% throttle / the blue zone and hold it until safe dropout.
details: Seven seconds is the safer training point; six seconds is the common practiced target.
Reducing throttle too late causes the classic overshoot or 'loop of shame'.
The ship must be both close enough and slow enough for a safe destination dropout; the HUD indicators show when both conditions are satisfied.
Advanced gravity-braking and Supercruise Assist tricks can be faster, but the 6-7 second method is the dependable baseline.

entries.topic: Supercruise Assist: Convenience vs Manual Travel
entries.ruleOfThumb: Supercruise Assist is primarily a convenience tool. Manual throttle control lets a CMDR travel at full speed for most of the leg and hand control back to SCA near the destination.
details: With manual throttle control enabled, SCA can maintain guidance while the pilot chooses the throttle setting.
A common workflow is full throttle during the cruise, then 75% near the 6-7 second mark.
SCA is not required for safe arrivals; it mainly reduces workload and can automatically manage the final dropout when correctly engaged.
Aggressive SCA shortcuts are advanced techniques and should not be the assistant's default recommendation for new pilots.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Use SCO as a short-duration in-system sprint, not as a normal cruise setting. It trades extreme acceleration for much higher fuel use, heat and ship-control workload.
details: SCO-capable Frame Shift Drives add an overcharge mode while already in supercruise.
Early SCO use caused major heat and structural stress; ships advertised as SCO-optimised handle the mode more comfortably than older hulls.
SCO is excellent for escaping deep gravity wells or cutting long in-system legs, but continuous use can burn fuel extremely quickly.
Keep an eye on heat, fuel and directional control and disengage SCO before the situation becomes unrecoverable.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Approach landable planets shallow enough to preserve Orbital Cruise, then let the game transition into Glide rather than diving vertically at the target.
details: Orbital Cruise is the high-speed planetary-approach regime between ordinary supercruise and normal flight.
For fastest lateral travel in Orbital Cruise, keep the pitch near the blue-zone horizon rather than pointing steeply downward.
Around 25 km is the normal lower boundary for Orbital Cruise on descent; a valid speed and angle transition the ship into Glide.
A bad approach angle can force an early dropout and leave a long normal-space flight to the surface target.

entries.topic: Standard White Dwarf & Neutron FSD Supercharging
entries.ruleOfThumb: With a normal compatible FSD and fuel scoop, a White Dwarf adds 50% range for one jump and a Neutron Star adds 300% range — making a neutron jump about 4x the ship's normal range.
details: The boost applies to the next hyperspace jump only.
A fuel scoop is required to collect the jet-cone particles that supercharge the FSD.
White dwarfs are generally poor travel boosters because their 50% benefit is small relative to the danger from their large exclusion zones.
Neutron stars are the basis of long-distance neutron-highway travel because their +300% boost is much more useful.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Enter a neutron jet from the side/shallow angle while travelling outward with the cone, never by diving toward the star. Stay in supercruise until the FSD reports that it is supercharged.
details: Aim for the outer portion of a jet cone and move in the same general direction as the particles, away from the neutron star.
The ship will buffet and yaw while inside the cone; that turbulence is expected.
Dropping to normal space inside a jet cone is extremely dangerous and can be fatal.
White-dwarf cones are much less forgiving because the exclusion zone occupies more of the usable cone.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Repeated jet-cone supercharging damages the Frame Shift Drive. Carry an AFMU on serious neutron-highway trips and repair the FSD before low integrity starts causing malfunctions.
details: Neutron and white-dwarf supercharging applies wear to the FSD over repeated uses.
An AFMU can repair the FSD in the field, but the FSD must be taken offline during the repair.
For long neutron trips, periodically check FSD integrity instead of waiting for a malfunction warning.
This is why a fuel scoop plus AFMU is standard equipment on dedicated neutron-highway exploration builds.

entries.topic: Caspian Explorer Mk II Supercharge Optimised FSD
entries.ruleOfThumb: Do not apply the standard 1.5x/4x jet-cone numbers to the Caspian Explorer's Mk II Supercharge Optimised FSD. It is a special-case drive with substantially stronger white-dwarf and neutron supercharge bonuses.
details: Current community documentation reports the Caspian-only Mk II Supercharge Optimised FSD at +200% from white dwarfs and +500% from neutron stars.
That corresponds to roughly 3x and 6x the unboosted jump range for the next jump, respectively.
The drive is specific to the Caspian Explorer and should not be treated as the current behaviour of ordinary SCO FSDs.
Because this is newer equipment, verify current live data when exact build planning depends on its final statistics.

entries.ruleOfThumb: FSD injections are one-jump synthesis boosts: Basic +25%, Standard +50%, Premium +100%. Save them for sparse-space route gaps and recovery rather than routine Bubble travel.
details: Basic FSD Injection uses Carbon, Vanadium and Germanium.
Standard adds higher-grade raw materials and gives +50% range.
Premium doubles the ship's normal jump range for one jump and requires rare raw materials including Yttrium and Polonium.
The boost is consumed by the next hyperspace jump, so confirm the destination before using scarce materials.

entries.ruleOfThumb: For very long trips, a neutron-highway route can beat ordinary fastest-route plotting by chaining neutron stars. Use a current external plotter such as Spansh when the in-game route is not aggressive enough.
details: Neutron-highway travel trades repeated FSD wear and more active flying for dramatically fewer jumps.
External neutron plotters can build routes around known neutron stars and refuelling needs.
Carry an AFMU, a fuel scoop and enough raw materials for emergency FSD injections before committing to remote neutron travel.
The route is only useful if the pilot is comfortable with safe cone entry; ordinary fastest routing is slower but lower workload.

entries.topic: Why the Galaxy Map Says Route Unavailable
entries.ruleOfThumb: When a route will not plot, check four things first: current laden jump range, fuel, star-density gaps, and permit-locked/restricted systems. Then try a nearer intermediate waypoint.
details: Cargo or module changes can reduce the ship below a required jump distance.
Near the galactic rim or other sparse regions, the next reachable star may simply be beyond current range.
Permit-locked systems can block direct routing through otherwise dense areas.
A shorter intermediate plot often reveals whether the problem is range, routing, restrictions or a temporary route-plotter issue.

entries.ruleOfThumb: Before a long trip, plan for fuel, FSD wear and route recovery: fit a scoop, know the scoopable-star filter, carry an AFMU for neutron use, and stock raw materials for at least emergency FSD injections.
details: A large fuel scoop reduces stationary refuelling time and makes long-distance travel much less tedious.
An AFMU becomes much more valuable if the route uses neutron boosts.
Raw materials for FSD Injection can turn an otherwise impossible sparse-space jump into a recoverable situation.
Verify that the destination is not permit-locked and that the ship can actually reach the local star density before leaving the last easy support point.
commonMistakes: Starting a neutron-highway trip without an AFMU.
Filtering out scoopable stars without noticing.
Planning from an unladen build and then loading cargo.
Using a premium FSD injection before confirming the selected jump.
Treating a White Dwarf like a low-risk neutron star.
